# Container-aware Java memory options with Spring Boot

A working Java container image is not enough: the JVM must derive its memory
ergonomics from the container limit and leave headroom for non-heap process
memory. This example compares fixed heap settings with percentage-based sizing
on the host and in a memory-limited container. You will inspect the computed
heap values and verify the different results in a Spring Boot image.

This is a focused example of JVM command-line options; it does not cover every
aspect of running Java in containers. For a more holistic Spring Boot example,
see [all-in-one-spring-boot](../all-in-one-spring-boot/).

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- inspect the JVM’s host and container memory ergonomics;
- compare fixed `-Xmx` sizing with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` sizing;
- verify the effective heap limit in a Spring Boot container; and
- explain why a heap percentage is not a substitute for measuring total process
  memory.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) runtime

- [Dive](https://github.com/wagoodman/dive), or other similar tool, to analyse
  the container image.

### Oracle Container Registry access

Before pulling an Oracle Java base image, sign in to Oracle Container Registry
and accept the terms for the
[Oracle Java JDK repository](https://container-registry.oracle.com/ords/ocr/ba/java/jdk).

1. Accept the Oracle Container Registry terms.

2. Authenticate your container engine with your own Oracle Container Registry
   username and authentication token.

   Pass the token through standard input so it is neither recorded in shell
   history nor copied into the project or image layers. If you use Podman, use
   its equivalent `login --password-stdin` command.

   ```shell
   docker login container-registry.oracle.com \
     --username 'ALBERT.ATTARD@ORACLE.COM' \
     --password-stdin < ~/.ocr/auth-token
   ```

   This should print the login succeeded message.

   ```
   Login Succeeded!
   ```

3. Verify that the container engine can pull and run the Oracle Java JDK image.

   ```shell
   docker run --rm 'container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' java --version
   ```

   Docker pulls the image if necessary, then prints the Java runtime version.

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   ```

## The artefacts to inspect

The Spring Boot application is packaged as
`target/java-command-line-options-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar`. Both container
Dockerfiles copy that same JAR and use `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS` to make the JVM
configuration visible at image-build time. The adjusted image uses percentage
sizing; the default image relies on JVM ergonomics.

```dockerfile
FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
WORKDIR "/opt/app"

ARG JAR_FILE="./target/java-command-line-options-spring-boot-*.jar"
COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

ENV JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="-XX:MinRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XshowSettings:vm"

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

## Build the application

Build the application once to create the controlled JAR input used by both
Spring Boot image variants later in the walkthrough.

1. Build the application

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── java-command-line-options-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── java-command-line-options-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. (*Optional*) Run the packaged application

   This starts the JAR outside a container. A successful endpoint response
   establishes that the application artefact works before its runtime layout is
   changed by container packaging.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/java-command-line-options-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote. A JSON response confirms that the packaged service is
   running and can serve its endpoint.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Mark Twain",
     "id": 119,
     "quote": "Age is an issue of mind over matter. If you don’t mind, it doesn’t matter."
   }
   ```

   Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Guided walkthrough

This walkthrough first establishes the JVM’s memory ergonomics on the host, then
repeats the inspection in a memory-limited container. It compares fixed heap
sizing with percentage-based sizing and applies both approaches to the same
Spring Boot application image.

Run the commands from this example directory. Treat the reported heap values as
observations for your JVM, host, and container runtime—not as production sizing
recommendations.

### Host JVM ergonomics

Before introducing a container limit, inspect how the JVM sizes its heap from
the memory available on the host. You will record the host memory, inspect the
JVM’s default heap ergonomics, then compare three explicit sizing approaches:
`-Xmx`, `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`, and `-XX:MaxRAM`.

The resulting values establish the baseline for the container walkthrough. They
also show that a maximum heap is only one part of the JVM process memory budget.

1. Determine the host memory

   Record this only as a baseline. The following JVM commands should report a
   maximum heap that reflects the host memory on this machine.

   ```shell
   case "$(uname -s)" in
     Darwin)
       bytes=$(sysctl -n hw.memsize)
       echo "$((bytes / 1024 / 1024 / 1024))GB"
       ;;
     Linux)
       kb=$(awk '/^MemTotal:/ { print $2 }' /proc/meminfo)
       echo "$((kb / 1024 / 1024))GB"
       ;;
     *)
       echo "Unsupported OS: $(uname -s)" >&2
       exit 1
       ;;
   esac
   ```

   This machine has 32GB of RAM

   ```
   30GB
   ```

2. Determine Java default memory limits (using the `-XshowSettings:vm` and
   `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` options)

   ```shell
   java \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   This will print the VM settings, which values vary depending on the version
   of Java and the host memory. Please note that the VM settings are printed to
   the stderr and not stdout.

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   VM settings:
       Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 7.72G
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   ```

   With this JVM configuration, ergonomics select a maximum heap of roughly 25%
   of the memory visible to the JVM. `MaxRAMPercentage` defaults to 25; the
   older `MaxRAMFraction` flag is deprecated. Treat the displayed result as
   evidence for this JVM and host, rather than a universal sizing rule.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal \
     --version \
     | grep -Ei 'maxheapsize|maxram'
   ```

   The memory settings

   ```
      size_t MaxHeapSize                              = 8292139008                                {product} {ergonomic}
    uint64_t MaxRAM                                   = 137438953472                           {pd product} {default}
      double MaxRAMPercentage                         = 25.000000                                 {product} {default}
      size_t SoftMaxHeapSize                          = 8292139008                             {manageable} {ergonomic}
   ```

3. Adjust the memory limits using `-Xmx###`

   One option is to use the `-Xmx###` (and `-Xms###`) options to adjust the
   maximum heap value. Note that Java uses other memory, such as the stack
   (one per thread), while the `-Xmx###` option only limits the heap.

   ```shell
   java \
     -Xmx1G -Xms1G \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   The Java version and VM settings

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   VM settings:
       Min. Heap Size: 1.00G
       Max. Heap Size: 1.00G
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   ```

   ```shell
   java \
     -Xmx1G -Xms1G \
     -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal \
     --version \
     | grep -Ei 'maxheapsize|maxram'
   ```

   The memory settings

   ```
      size_t MaxHeapSize                              = 1073741824                                {product} {command line}
    uint64_t MaxRAM                                   = 137438953472                           {pd product} {default}
      double MaxRAMPercentage                         = 25.000000                                 {product} {default}
      size_t SoftMaxHeapSize                          = 1073741824                             {manageable} {ergonomic}
   ```

4. Adjust the memory limits using `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=###`

   The `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=###` instructs Java to set the heap size a
   percentage of the available memory.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   The Java version and VM settings

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   VM settings:
       Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 23.17G
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   ```

   ```shell

     -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal \
     --version \
   ```

5. Adjust the memory limits using `-XX:MaxRAM=###`

   The `-XX:MaxRAM=###` sets the host memory limit for Java. When provided,
   Java will use this value as the host memory and will derive the other values
   based on this. For example, if the host has 16G of RAM, with `-XX:MaxRAM=4G`,
   Java limits the heap to 1G.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:MaxRAM=4G \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   The Java version and VM settings

   ```

   VM settings:
       Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 1.00G
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   ```

   ```shell
     -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal \
     --version \
     | grep -Ei 'maxheapsize|maxram'
   ```

   ```
      size_t SoftMaxHeapSize                          = 1073741824                             {manageable} {ergonomic}
   ```

   Please note that `-Xmx###` takes precedence over `-XX:MaxRAM=##`.

   ```shell
   java \
     -Xmx512M -Xms512M \
     -XX:MaxRAM=4G \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   ```

    uint64_t MaxRAM                                   = 4294967296                             {pd product} {command line}
   ```

### Container memory ergonomics

This section repeats the JVM memory inspection inside a container limited to 1
GiB. You will compare the memory reported by standard operating-system tools
with the cgroup limit that constrains the container, then inspect how the JVM
derives its default heap from that limit.

You will also compare fixed `-Xmx` sizing with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` and
`-XX:MaxRAM`, observing which settings scale with the container limit and which
override JVM ergonomics.

1. Determine the memory available to the container

   `free` reports memory from the kernel perspective; it does not reliably show
   the container’s cgroup limit. Compare its output with the cgroup value next.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     free
   ```

   This reports memory visible from the kernel perspective, not necessarily the
   container limit.

   ```
                  total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
   Mem:        32388656     2525740     1393752       57488    29015940    29862916
   Swap:        5331964           0     5331964
   ```

   The memory available in a container can be determined from the control groups
   (cgroup) file: `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max`.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max
   ```

   This prints 1G (in bytes value).

   ```
   1073741824
   ```

   The next command converts the cgroup value to GiB. It is a convenience
   display, so expect truncation rather than an exact decimal value.

   ```shell
   echo "$(expr $(docker run --rm --memory=1G container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max | sed 's/\r//g') / $((1024**3)))GB"
   ```

   This prints the same value in GB.

   ```
   1GB
   ```

   ![Container Memory](./assets/images/Container%20Memory.png)

2. Determine Java default memory limits (using the `-XshowSettings:vm` and
   `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` options)

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     java \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   This will print the VM settings, which values vary depending on the version
   of Java and the container memory.

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   VM settings:
       Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 247.50M
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   ```

   Note that when using the G1 GC, the JVM adjusts the heap as 25% of the total
   memory.

   ![Default Heap Size](./assets/images/Default%20Heap%20Size.png)

   This is determined by the (*deprecated*) `MaxRAMFraction` option, which is
   set to `4` by default or the (*newer*) `MaxRAMPercentage` option which is set
   to `25%`.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     java \
     -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal \
     --version \
     | grep -Ei 'maxheapsize|maxram'
   ```

   This will print the VM settings, which values vary depending on the version
   of Java and the container memory.

   ```
      size_t MaxHeapSize                              = 268435456                                 {product} {ergonomic}
    uint64_t MaxRAM                                   = 137438953472                           {pd product} {default}
      double MaxRAMPercentage                         = 25.000000                                 {product} {default}
      size_t SoftMaxHeapSize                          = 268435456                              {manageable} {ergonomic}
   ```

3. Adjust the memory limits using `-Xmx###`

   One option is to use the `-Xmx###` (and `-Xms###`) options to adjust the
   maximum heap value. Note that Java uses other memory, such as the stack (one
   per thread), while the `-Xmx###` option only limits the heap.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     java \
     -Xmx512M -Xms512M \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   The memory settings

   set the container memory to 2G, will Java take advantage of the available

   ![Set Heap Size though Xmx does not scale](./assets/images/Set%20Heap%20Size%20though%20Xmx%20does%20not%20scale.png)

4. Adjust the memory limits using `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=###`

   The `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=###` instructs Java to set the heap size a
   percentage of the available memory.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     java \
     -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   The Java version and VM settings

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   VM settings:
       Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 742.44M
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   ```

   Unlike `-Xmx`, `MaxRAMPercentage` scales the maximum heap with the memory
   visible to the JVM. At 75%, the heap consumes up to 75% of that memory; the
   remaining headroom must accommodate metaspace, code cache, thread stacks,
   direct buffers, native libraries, and the application’s native allocations.

   ![Set Heap Size though MaxRAMPercentage](./assets/images/Set%20Heap%20Size%20though%20MaxRAMPercentage.png)

   The screenshots show the scaling behaviour, not a recommended production
   value. Whether 25%, 75%, or another value is appropriate depends on the
   application’s threads, native memory use, workload, and container limit.

   ![Set Heap Size though MaxRAMPercentage scale with container](./assets/images/Set%20Heap%20Size%20though%20MaxRAMPercentage%20scale%20with%20container.png)

   Please note that the `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` option takes precedence over
   `-XX:MaxRAMFraction` option.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     java \
     -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 \
     -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal \
     --version \
     | grep -Ei 'maxheapsize|maxram'
   ```


   Please note that `-Xmx###` takes precedence over `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=##`.

5. Adjust the memory limits using `-XX:MaxRAM=###`

   The `-XX:MaxRAM=###` sets the host memory limit for Java. When provided,
   Java will use this value as the host memory and will derive the other values
   based on this. For example, if the host has 16G of RAM, with `-XX:MaxRAM=4G`,
   Java limits the heap for 4G, that 1G.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     java \
     -XX:MaxRAM=512M \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   The Java version and VM settings

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   VM settings:
       Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 123.75M
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   ```

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     java \
     -XX:MaxRAM=512M \
     -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal \
     --version \
     | grep -Ei 'maxheapsize|maxram'
   ```

   The memory settings

   ```
      size_t MaxHeapSize                              = 134217728                                 {product} {ergonomic}
    uint64_t MaxRAM                                   = 536870912                              {pd product} {command line}
      double MaxRAMPercentage                         = 25.000000                                 {product} {default}
      size_t SoftMaxHeapSize                          = 134217728                              {manageable} {ergonomic}
   ```

   Please note that `-Xmx###` takes precedence over `-XX:MaxRAM=##`.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 \
     java \
     -Xmx256M -Xms256M \
     -XX:MaxRAM=512M \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     --version
   ```

   ```
    uint64_t MaxRAM                                   = 536870912                              {pd product} {command line}
   ```

### Java 8 update comparison

Java 8u351 and 8u361 are both post-8u191 releases, so they should detect the 1
GiB cgroup limit. This sequence therefore verifies container awareness in those
updates; it does not demonstrate the pre-8u191 behaviour that used host memory.
A genuine comparison with that historical behaviour needs different image tags,
which this review does not change.

```shell
docker run \
  --rm \
  --memory=1G \
  container-registry.oracle.com/java/serverjre:8u351 \
  java \
  -XshowSettings:vm \
  -version
```

Expect a maximum heap of roughly 25% of the 1 GiB container limit, not a heap
derived from the host memory.

```
VM settings:
    Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 6.86G
    Ergonomics Machine Class: server
    Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM

java version "1.8.0_351"
Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 1.8.0_351-b10)
Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.351-b10, mixed mode)
```

`-XX:MaxRAM` overrides the memory value used by JVM ergonomics. It is useful for
demonstrating precedence, but it is not a reason to retain an obsolete Java 8
update; use a supported JDK release instead.

```shell
docker run \
  --rm \
  --memory=1G \
  container-registry.oracle.com/java/serverjre:8u351 \
  java \
  -XX:MaxRAM=1G \
  -XshowSettings:vm \
  -version
```

Java uses `-XX:MaxRAM=###` as the input to heap ergonomics, even though this JVM
would otherwise detect the container limit.

```
VM settings:
    Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 228.00M
    Ergonomics Machine Class: server
    Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM

java version "1.8.0_351"
Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 1.8.0_351-b10)
Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.351-b10, mixed mode)
```

Java 8u361 should produce the same container-aware result. It remains an old
release; use a currently supported JDK release in real deployments.

```shell
docker run \
  --rm \
  --memory=1G \
  container-registry.oracle.com/java/serverjre:8u361 \
  java \
  -XshowSettings:vm \
  -version
```

The heap is allocated only 25% of the memory available to the container.

```
VM settings:
    Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 247.50M
    Ergonomics Machine Class: server
    Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM

java version "1.8.0_361"
Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 1.8.0_361-b09)
Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.361-b09, mixed mode)
```

Do not treat this section as a recommendation to deploy either Java 8 image.

### Enterprise Performance Pack

This section demonstrates how to build a container image based on Enterprise
Performance Pack (EPP) and load into the local container registry. For a
comprehensive description of how to create a multi-platform container image for
EPP, please refer to the
[Create a multi-platform container image with Java SE Subscription Enterprise Performance Pack](https://inside.java/2023/06/12/multiplatform-containers-javaepp/)
article.

1. Download EPP from the
   [Oracle Java Downloads page](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#jepp).

   Save the RPM files under the `./containers/binaries` directory.

   Verify that the RPM files are under the `./containers/binaries` directory.

   ```shell
   tree -P '*.rpm' './containers'
   ```

   The EPP RPM.

   ```
   ./containers
   └── binaries
       ├── jdk-8u503-perf-linux-aarch64.rpm
       └── jdk-8u503-perf-linux-x64.rpm

   2 directories, 2 files
   ```

2. Build the container image

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-EPP' \
     --tag 'epp:503' \
     --load \
     './containers'
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the image is loaded in the local container registry.

   ```shell
   docker image list epp
   ```

   The images in the local repository

   ```
   REPOSITORY     TAG         IMAGE ID      CREATED       SIZE
   localhost/epp  503         df69da01184e  1 second ago  400 MB
   ```

3. Run the container image

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --memory=1G \
     epp:503 \
     java \
     -XshowSettings:vm \
     -version
   ```

   EPP is able to detect the container limits and adjusts accordingly.

   ```
   VM settings:
       Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 247.50M
       Ergonomics Machine Class: server
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM

   java version "1.8.0_503"
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 1.8.0_503-perf-7-b01)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 17.0.20+1-perf-7, mixed mode, sharing)
   ```

### Apply the settings to a Spring Boot image

This section applies the memory-sizing approaches to the Spring Boot
application. You will build the same application JAR into two container images:
one that uses the JVM’s default container-aware ergonomics and one that sets a
75% maximum heap percentage.

By running both images with the same 1 GiB memory limit and inspecting their
startup output, you will compare the effective heap settings. The comparison
makes the headroom trade-off visible; it does not establish a production-ready
memory configuration.

1. (*Optional*) Verify that the build produced the JAR used by both images.

   ```shell
   tree -P '*.jar' --prune './target'
   ```

   The application JAR file

   ```
   ./target
   └── java-command-line-options-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

2. Review the adjusted-heap container file
   (`./containers/Dockerfile-Adjusted-Heap`)

   The container applies the JVM options through the `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS`
   environment variable. This keeps the image entrypoint focused on the
   application launch command while still making the JVM options visible in the
   container definition.

   The JVM options are:

   - `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0`: sets the maximum Java heap as a percentage of
     the memory available to the JVM. In this example, the maximum heap can grow
     up to 75% of the container memory limit.
   - `-XX:MinRAMPercentage=75.0`: sets the minimum heap percentage used by JVM
     ergonomics for small memory sizes. It does not reserve all container memory
     for the heap, and it should not be treated as a replacement for deliberate
     `-Xms` sizing.
   - `-XshowSettings:vm`: prints VM settings during startup. This is useful in
     the workshop because it shows the computed heap size, but it is usually a
     diagnostic option rather than a production logging default.

   The 75% value is a demonstration default, not a production recommendation.
   Validate it against the application workload because heap memory is only part
   of the process memory used by the JVM.

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
   WORKDIR "/opt/app"

   ARG JAR_FILE="./target/java-command-line-options-spring-boot-*.jar"
   COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

   ENV JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="-XX:MinRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XshowSettings:vm"

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

3. Build the (adjusted heap) container image

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-Adjusted-Heap' \
     --tag 'demo:adjusted-heap' \
     --load \
     .
   ```

4. Run the container image

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --detach \
     --memory=1G \
     --name 'adjusted-heap' \
     --publish 8080:8080 \
     'demo:adjusted-heap'
   ```

   The startup output should show an estimated maximum heap of approximately 75%
   of the 1 GiB container limit. This confirms the configured ergonomic
   calculation; it does not measure the application’s total memory consumption.

   ```shell
   docker logs 'adjusted-heap' | head
   ```

   This application is using 75% of the container’s memory.

   ```
   NOTE: Picked up JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS: -XX:MinRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XshowSettings:vm
   VM settings:
       Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 742.44M
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   ```

5. Stop the container once ready.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'adjusted-heap'
   ```

6. Review the default-options container file
   (`./containers/Dockerfile-Default-Options`)

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
   WORKDIR "/opt/app"

   ARG JAR_FILE="./target/java-command-line-options-spring-boot-*.jar"
   COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

   ENV JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="-XshowSettings:vm"

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

7. Build the (default options) container image

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-Default-Options' \
     --tag 'demo:default-options' \
     --load \
     .
   ```

8. Run the container image

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --detach \
     --memory=1G \
     --name 'default-options' \
     --publish 8080:8080 \
     'demo:default-options'
   ```

   The startup output should show the JVM’s default estimated maximum heap,
   roughly 25% of the 1 GiB container limit for this configuration. Compare it
   with the adjusted image rather than treating either number as an approved
   production size.

   ```shell
   docker logs 'default-options' | head
   ```

   This application is using 25% of memory available to the container.

   ```
   NOTE: Picked up JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS: -XshowSettings:vm
   VM settings:
       Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 247.50M
       Using VM: Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
   ```

   The comparison makes the trade-off visible: the default leaves more non-heap
   headroom, while the adjusted image gives the heap a larger share of the same
   limit.

9. Stop the container once ready.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'default-options'
   ```

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- The JVM can derive its heap ergonomics from a container cgroup limit; inspect
  the effective settings rather than assuming host-memory behaviour.
- `-Xmx` fixes the maximum heap, while `MaxRAMPercentage` allows that maximum to
  scale with the memory available to the JVM.
- A larger heap percentage can help heap-intensive workloads, but it reduces
  headroom for non-heap, native, and application memory.
- Use a supported JDK and validate the chosen settings with the deployed
  workload and actual container limits.
